what_taken: Argues from evolutionary ecology and energy dissipation that humanity is in advanced overshoot and has exceeded long-term human carrying capacity (p. 509). Population reached eight billion in November 2022 and real gross world product rose over 100-fold in two centuries (p. 515). Predicts a major population correction within the twenty-first century (p. 509); cites long-term carrying capacity estimates of 100 million to 3 billion (p. 522).

Carrying capacity K is defined as the average maximum sustainable population for a habitat (p. 514). The 100 million and 3 billion figures are global, are cited from two outside sources and are not computed in the paper, so they sit beside the global debate and not beside the Australian 9 to 100 million range in the B OUTLINE.

file_ok: yes: Swiader, Lin, Szewranski, Kazak, Iha, van Hoof, Belcakova and Altiok 2020, Environ. Sci. Policy 105:56-74 (p. 56), CC BY-NC-ND
what_taken: Uses ecological footprint (EF) and biocapacity (BC) to assess environmental carrying capacity of Wroclaw, Poland, for 2016, comparing a top-down EF, a bottom-up carbon footprint and a hybrid of the two (pp. 56, 65-66).
